principles.text: Shorting a bounce into the declining 21 EMA has a higher success rate than shorting at the declining 9; the 9 is still a good short when it converges with another level (50 EMA, prior candle high, prior swing low, anchored VWAP). Using the declining 9 alone has a lower win rate.
Prefers to short while the stock is still within its base, near converging EMAs, rather than when it is already breaking down and extended.

Calls his early short his mistake: he should have waited for a longer (about 3-day) bounce into the declining 9 EMA. Shorting at several stacked resistances (unfilled gap, weekly EMA, flat 50) gives a better edge than shorting early in the morning.
Trends start on the lowest timeframe (1-min -> 15-min -> hourly -> daily), so he enters on intraday candle breakouts or breakdowns rather than buying falling knives.
On a high-conviction trade, accept the risk and pull the trigger. If hesitating, don't take it; come back in a few days to see whether the entry worked and take away what made it work or fail.

With a tight stop (<1%) on a fast stock (ADR >4-5%) he keeps normal 20-25% sizing and risks only ~0.1-0.15%; he does not size up for a 'perfect' tight-stop entry because gap risk can destroy the account.
Will not risk anything like 10% of the account on one trade, however good it looks.
Sizes about the same as when the account was small (maybe up to ~30%); larger sizing in fewer positions only raises variance, so he does not recommend it.
Heavy short exposure without profit cushion is risky: a gap up against an overexposed book can mean a >5% drawdown on the gap alone.
Journal every trade by hand (entries, exits, shares, P&L); the effort of manual entry is a check on overtrading.
Trade a small account as if managing a $100M portfolio, to build habits that scale.

Routine: about an hour after waking going through charts, screens and the watchlist; about 30 min before the open, review pre-market movers and the watchlist for gaps into levels for pullback entries. Usually watches only until ~12:30-1pm, longer on volatile or opportunity-rich days.
